title: HTML Elements & Attributes
summary: Elements mark content and attributes add information about that content.

subtopics.title: The document frame
subtopics.explanation:
An opening tag begins most HTML elements, such as `

`. It can include attributes that configure the element. It is like opening a labeled container. Some elements are void elements and do not wrap content, so learn their form instead of adding a closing tag where HTML does not use one. In practice, use an anchor with `href` for navigation so the destination is announced and can be opened in a new tab. For example, use a label element with `for` matching the input ID.

subtopics.title: Important pieces
subtopics.explanation:
A closing tag ends many elements that wrap content, such as `

`. Correct nesting helps the browser build the intended page tree. It is like closing a box before putting it inside another. Browsers may repair malformed markup, but the repaired structure can differ from what you expected. In practice, an image’s `alt` describes its purpose; `src` tells the browser which file to load. For example, give an external anchor a real destination instead of a click handler on a span.

subtopics.title: Page information
subtopics.explanation: Some elements, such as ``, do not wrap text or child elements. These are void elements. It is like a picture inserted into a document rather than a folder holding more pages. Add the attributes the element needs, including a useful `alt` value for images. In practice, a button’s `type` can prevent an unrelated form submission. For example, specify `type="button"` for a non-submit control inside a form.

subtopics.title: Content structure
subtopics.explanation: Attributes provide extra information inside an opening tag. A link uses `href` for its destination; an image uses `src` for its file. They are like labeled fields on a form. Use attributes supported by the element and choose values that match the content’s purpose. In practice, a `lang` attribute can help a screen reader choose pronunciation rules. For example, use `alt` to convey an image’s purpose, not its visual inventory.

subtopics.title: Good habits
subtopics.explanation: Quote attribute values, such as `href="/about"`, even when the value contains no spaces. Quotes make boundaries clear and prevent punctuation from changing the value. It is like putting a label inside quotation marks on a form. Use semantic HTML so browsers and assistive technology know what each element does. In practice, choose a semantic element before adding ARIA to a generic container. For example, keep attribute values quoted so boundaries stay clear when they change.

foundations.overview: HTML elements describe the structure and meaning of page content. Tags mark where elements begin and end; attributes add details such as a link destination or image text. Think of an element as a labeled container and its attributes as notes attached to that container. Use semantic elements where possible, close elements correctly, and quote attribute values.
foundations.whyItMatters: Correct elements and attributes provide built-in browser behavior and accessible meaning. They reduce the amount of custom interaction code a team must maintain.
commonUseCases: Add an href destination to a link.
Give an image a source and an appropriate alternative text value.
Use semantic elements to expose a button or navigation region.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Any element can become a button with a click handler.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A native button includes focus, keyboard activation, and accessibility behavior that a generic container lacks.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Attributes can be added without regard to the element.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Attributes have defined meanings and are valid only in appropriate contexts.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Browsers always display malformed nesting as intended.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Browsers attempt repairs, but the resulting structure may not match the author’s assumptions.

visualExplorer.title: Anatomy of an element
visualExplorer.caption: How a tag, its attributes, and its content combine into a single configured element.

config.intro: Every HTML element is built from the same few parts. Here's how they fit together.

steps.name: Opening tag
steps.detail: Starts the element: the element name in angle brackets, e.g. <a>.

steps.name: Attributes
steps.detail: name="value" pairs inside the opening tag that configure it, e.g. href="...".

steps.name: Content
steps.detail: The text or nested elements between the opening and closing tags.

steps.name: Closing tag
steps.detail: Ends the element with a slash, e.g. — omitted for void elements.

steps.name: Void elements
steps.detail:
Self-contained tags like and
have no content and no closing tag.

steps.name: Nesting
steps.detail: Elements live inside one another and must close in the order they opened.

codeLab.title: Add the right attributes
codeLab.instructions: The link has no destination, the image is missing its source and alt text, and the submit button should be disabled. Add href to the link, src and alt to the image, and the disabled boolean attribute to the button.
codeLab.expectedOutput: A working link pointing to a URL, an image with a source and descriptive alt text, and a disabled submit button.
